Irony is a rhetorical and literary mode in which the speaker or text implies meaning opposite to, or sharply different from, what is literally said, creating a gap between appearance and reality. It ranges from simple sarcasm, where you say the opposite of what you mean, to dramatic irony where the audience knows something the characters do not, to situational irony where reality contradicts expectation. Irony has been essential to literature across genres and centuries, serving as both a tool for critique and a source of philosophical complexity.

Verbal irony occurs when what is said contradicts what is meant. Sarcasm is irony used for mockery or contempt. Dramatic irony arises when the audience or reader knows more than the characters on stage. They see the full implications of the characters' words and actions. Situational irony occurs when reality inverts expectation. Oedipus kills his father while trying to prevent it. The weather refuses to cooperate with lovers' plans. Irony is central to comedy, which exploits incongruity and the audience's superior knowledge. It is also fundamental to satire, which uses ironic praise to expose folly.

Romantic irony, developed in the early nineteenth century, emphasizes the gap between human aspiration and reality. The subject recognizes the futility of desire yet persists in desiring. Postmodern irony is irony about irony: the simultaneous commitment to and detachment from meaning, sincerity and skepticism. It is a mode of engagement without earnestness. Excessive irony can collapse into cynicism. If everything is ironized, nothing is affirmed, and critique loses force.

Comedy depends on irony as essential to comic effect. The audience's sense of superiority creates laughter. Satire uses ironic praise as its primary weapon. Irony makes critique bite. Postmodernism made irony its dominant mode of art and literature. Wit depends on verbal cleverness that often relies on ironic or unexpected juxtaposition. Rhetoric, the study of persuasion and language, recognizes irony as a fundamental rhetorical device. Greek drama is the ancient source of dramatic irony as a literary principle. Sarcasm is the crude, personal version of irony where contempt is made explicit through inversion. Irony's power lies in creating multiple registers of meaning simultaneously, allowing writers to address multiple audiences and to say one thing while meaning another.
